ch17.title: The Last Days in the Temple
ch17.b001: A Question on the Downhill Road
ch17.b002: On Monday morning the twelve gathered, as had been arranged, at the home of Simon in Bethany. After a short conference the Master set out for Jerusalem. As they went down the western slope of Olivet he walked in front, and the twelve kept close behind him. No one spoke. They had not yet come back to themselves after the day before. The hosannas were still ringing in their ears, and in their chests was the hollow feeling of a great shout that had led nowhere. On top of that, the Master had told them they were to do no public teaching at all during this Passover week, and the instruction seemed to have set an invisible distance between them and him.
ch17.b003: The spring sun struck the white walls of the temple across the Kidron valley until they dazzled the eye. The almond trees along the path had shed their blossoms and were pushing out pale new leaves. Bands of pilgrims were walking down the same road, and their singing ran down the hillside ahead of them.
ch17.b004: Eleven of the twelve carried the same question in their hearts: What will the Master do today? Judas Iscariot carried a different one. What shall I do? Shall I keep following, or shall I draw back? And if I draw back, how do I leave?
ch17.b005: Judas turned that question over with every step. The night before he had decided to stay one more day, and that day was today. He watched the Master’s back as he walked ahead: the worn cloak, the solid shoulders. It was the same back he had first seen at Tarichea. But the eyes with which Judas looked at it had changed. He knew this, and he laid it at the Master’s door. It is not I who have changed, he told himself. That man has made me into this. That was how he reckoned it, and the reckoning made him comfortable.
ch17.b006: Andrew walked at the very rear of the group. He was the chief, and the chief’s place was behind, where he could see them all. All the day before he had had no leisure to weigh the shouting of the crowd. He had been too busy watching Peter, James and John, and Simon Zelotes, afraid that the fever of the day would sweep them into something rash. He knew that some of the twelve were carrying swords, and it troubled him; he did not know that his own brother Peter was one of them. And now his eyes kept drifting to Judas’s back. He remembered the face of Judas at Simon’s feast two nights before, when Judas had crossed over to him and urged him to rebuke the waste. Whatever had been seething beneath that face, Andrew had not yet found a name for it. Again he said nothing to anyone. Not to speak of what he was not sure of — that was his way. For the first time, he was not sure his way was right.
ch17.b008: About nine o’clock they reached the temple. The Master went to the large court where he so often taught, greeted the believers who had been waiting for him, and stepped up onto one of the teaching platforms. The apostles drew back a little way and waited.
ch17.b009: The court was a market. Pens of sacrificial animals lined the walls, and coins rang on the tables of the money-changers. The temple dues could be paid only in the Jewish shekel, so pilgrims from far provinces arrived with more than twenty kinds of money and had to change it, losing a commission every time. There had been seasons when a pair of doves cost as much as a week’s wages. The larger share of all that profit found its way into the hands of the high-priestly families.
ch17.b010: Nathaniel frowned in the din. He was a man of Cana, proud of his country and proud of his people, and at the center of that pride stood this temple. Yet here, in its very courts, the lowing of cattle and the haggling of traders and the clink of coins were drowning out the voices of prayer. A joke came to him: even the God of Abraham would have to change his money here. He did not say it aloud. It was too sad to laugh at.
ch17.b011: The Master was just about to begin when two things happened at once. At a nearby exchange table a loud and angry quarrel broke out over a Jew from Alexandria who claimed he had been overcharged. At the same moment a drove of some hundred bullocks was being driven from one pen to another, and their bellowing tore the air. And close by, a simple Galilean, a man the Master had once talked with, was being jostled and mocked by a knot of superior Judeans.
ch17.b012: The Master looked on all of it for a while in silence. Then he stepped down from the platform.
ch17.b013: The apostles could only stare at what followed. He went up to the boy who was driving the cattle, took the whip of cords from his hand, and drove the animals out of the temple. Nor was that the end of it. While thousands watched, holding their breath, he walked with great dignity to the farthest pen and threw open the gate of every stall, and the penned beasts poured out. Then the pilgrims, roaring, surged toward the bazaars and started tipping over the money-changers’ tables. Within five minutes every trace of trade had been swept from the court. By the time the Roman guards came running, all was already quiet.
ch17.b014: The Master went back to the platform and told the people that they had seen this day what the Scriptures had written: that this house was meant to be called a house of prayer for all nations, and they had made it a den of robbers. The crowd broke into hosannas. A throng of young people stepped forward and sang hymns of thanks. For the rest of that day the people themselves stood guard at every archway and would not let anyone carry so much as an empty vessel across the courts.
ch17.b015: Nathaniel could not move from his place beside the platform. Neither could any of the others. Not one of them lifted a finger. If it had been yesterday, Nathaniel thought — if this had come at the end of yesterday’s shouting — we would have been ready. Simon Zelotes would have led the way, and Peter would have followed. But today the Master had done it at a moment no one expected, and he had done it alone. Nathaniel did not think that was an accident. The Master had left no opening for their swords.
ch17.b016: For an instant Judas Iscariot’s heart leapt. At last? He looked at the overturned tables and the scattered coins. This was power. At last the man had put himself forward. But what happened that afternoon broke his hopes again, one by one. When elders from the Sanhedrin came and asked by what authority he did these things, the Master asked them in return whether the baptism of John had come from heaven or from men, and when they said they did not know, he told them that neither would he tell them. A clever answer. But it was not a proclamation. Then came the parable of the two sons, the parable of the tenants of the vineyard, the parable of the wedding feast. When someone asked for a sign, the Master pointed to his own body and said that if this temple were destroyed he would raise it up in three days. People shook their heads. The apostles did not understand him either. Judas listened and sneered inwardly. Another riddle.
ch17.b017: Toward four o’clock the Master gave the sign to leave the temple. On the way up Olivet he told Andrew, Philip, and Thomas that on the morrow they should set up a camp nearer the city, where they could stay for the rest of Passover week. That night, once again, it was a silent band that climbed the western slope. The morning’s cleansing had raised their hope that the Master would at last reveal his power, but the afternoon had let that hope run out flat. They hardly slept. Even the twins understood now that something was rushing toward its end.
ch17.b019: At about seven o’clock on Tuesday morning the Master met the apostles, the women’s evangelistic corps, and some two dozen prominent disciples at Simon’s house. He said good-bye to Lazarus, giving him the counsel that would soon send him fleeing to Philadelphia; he said good-bye to old Simon; and he gave the women’s corps his parting advice. He never formally addressed them again.
ch17.b020: Then he greeted each of the twelve in turn.
ch17.b021: Andrew came first. The Master stood before him and told him not to be dismayed by what was about to happen. He was to keep a firm hold on his brethren, and see to it that they did not find him downcast.
ch17.b022: Andrew nodded. It was the second half of the charge that stayed in his ears longer than the first. See that they do not find you downcast. The Master knew that he was downcast. He knew the doubts and the unease Andrew had confided to no one. And he had not told him to get rid of them. He had told him only to carry them alone and hold on to his brothers. Andrew knew the load was heavy. He also knew that it fitted him. He had lived that way all his life.
ch17.b023: The Master went on down the line. He told Peter not to trust in the arm of flesh or in weapons of steel, but to build himself on the everlasting rock. Peter’s hand moved without thinking toward the side of his cloak, then stopped. Andrew saw the movement and did not understand it. To James the Master said that he must not waver because of outward appearances. To John he said that he should be gentle, should love even his enemies, and should remember how much had been entrusted to him. Nathaniel he told not to judge by appearances, and to hold fast to his faith even when everything seemed to vanish. Philip he told to stand unshaken even when he could not see the way. He reminded Matthew of the mercy that had received him into the kingdom, and told him to let no one cheat him of his eternal reward; Matthew took the words with his head bowed. Thomas must walk for now by faith and not by sight. The twins were not to let what they could not understand crush them, but to be true to the affections of their hearts and stand by their brethren. To Simon Zelotes he said that he might be crushed by disappointment, yet his spirit would rise above it all.
ch17.b024: And then the Master stood in front of Judas Iscariot.
ch17.b025: Andrew held his breath. He could not have said why. The Master looked at Judas and told him that he had loved him, and that he had prayed Judas would love his brethren. He told him not to grow weary in well-doing, and warned him to beware of the slippery paths of flattery and the poisoned darts of ridicule.
ch17.b026: Judas bowed his head and received it. Nothing showed on his face. But when the word ridicule was spoken, his shoulders stiffened, very slightly. He remembered the hand of that Sadducee slapping his back at the city gate two days before. The Master could not know about that. Or could he? Judas pushed the question away. And of everything he had heard, he decided not to hear the words *I have loved you*. If he heard them, his accounts would not balance.
ch17.b027: Andrew laid that farewell beside the other eleven. The Master’s voice had been no different. It had been neither shorter nor longer. His gaze had been the same. And yet those words were like none he had said to anyone else. *I have loved you* — as though it were already past. And then the warning. Between those two, Andrew felt something settle in him, cold. He looked at Judas. Judas had already turned away and was retying the cord of the money bag.
ch17.b029: When the farewells were over, the Master left for Jerusalem with Andrew, Peter, James, and John, while the other apostles went to set up the new camp near Gethsemane. About halfway down the slope of Olivet he stopped and talked with the four for more than an hour. The subject was one Peter and James had been arguing over for days: the forgiveness of sin. The Master told them that when a man understands the inner impulses of his brother he will come to love him, and that when you love your brother you have already forgiven him.
ch17.b030: That morning in the temple one group after another tried to trap him. Was it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar? Whose wife, in the resurrection, would be the woman who had been married to seven brothers? Which was the greatest commandment? He turned aside each question. By noon no one was asking any more.
ch17.b031: At that hour Philip was in the market buying supplies for the new camp. Some Greek believers from Alexandria, Athens, and Rome came up to him and asked to see the Master. Philip was flustered. There was the instruction against public teaching, and these men were gentiles. He asked them to wait where they were and hurried to the home of Joseph of Arimathea, where he called Andrew away from his lunch. Andrew went back with Philip and brought the Greeks to Joseph’s house, and the Master received them. There he spoke of the grain of wheat that must fall into the earth and die if it is to bear much fruit, and then he paused. Those in the room felt that something had spoken to him.
ch17.b032: At Joseph’s table there was one empty place. Judas Iscariot was not there. Andrew noticed. A chief always counts heads. Judas had left with the others after the morning farewells to set up the camp, but by the time the others drifted in toward midday he had not appeared. Andrew supposed he had gone somewhere on business for the money bag. He wanted to suppose so.
ch17.b033: At that very hour Judas was eating lunch in a house in the city with some Sadducean relatives and friends. There, for the first time, he opened his heart. Jesus, he said, was a well-meaning dreamer and an idealist, but he was not the deliverer Israel had been waiting for. He would like to find a way to withdraw from the movement without losing face. Together they talked over how that might be done.
ch17.b034: His relatives were kind. They told him the Jewish rulers would welcome his return as a great event. Nothing would be too good for him. At last, they said, he could wash off the stain of his unfortunate entanglement with those unlearned Galileans. One relative smiled and remarked that this Jesus might be a well-meaning fanatic, but he was probably not quite sound of mind. Judas made no reply. He knew better than anyone how strong the Master was, how keen and how sound that mind. And yet the words were sweet in his ears. He held the sweetness in his mouth a little too long. *The slippery paths of flattery.* The phrase he had heard that morning surfaced for a moment, then sank into his wine cup.
ch17.b035: A little after two o’clock the Master came to the temple with eleven apostles, with Joseph, with the thirty Greeks, and with others, and began his last address. He told the people he had long been among them, proclaiming the Father’s love. The Father had dealt in mercy with this people for generations, he said, and even now he was holding out his hand. The apostles stood before him in silence.
ch17.b036: Judas returned to the temple court only after that appeal to mercy was finished. By the time he slipped in among them, the Master’s voice had changed. He was pronouncing woes upon the scribes and the Pharisees: they cleaned the outside of the cup while the inside was full of extortion and excess; they were like whitewashed tombs; they adorned the tombs of the prophets while they plotted to kill the one of whom the prophets had spoken. And then he cried out that Jerusalem stoned her prophets; that he would have gathered her children as a hen gathers her chicks, and she would not; and that now her house was left to her desolate.
ch17.b037: Listening, Judas made up his mind. It is finished. This man has broken with the rulers of the temple for good. Judas knew what the Sanhedrin would do when they heard of it, and he resolved not to be standing on the losing side. The first half of the address, the part in which the Master had offered mercy and forgiveness in the Father’s name even now, never reached him. Would he have been different had he heard it? No one could say. But that afternoon he walked out of the temple together with the other twelve, and no one thought anything of his late arrival.
ch17.b039: As they were leaving the temple, Matthew pointed at the buildings. Look at these great stones, he said, at this beautiful adornment — could all this really be thrown down? The Master told him the day was coming when not one stone would be left upon another.
ch17.b040: To avoid the crowds streaming along the Kidron valley, they climbed a little way up the western slope of Olivet and then followed a path toward their own camp above the public camping ground at Gethsemane. As they turned off the Bethany road they looked back. The temple was blazing in the setting sun as if it had caught fire. Presently the lights of the city came on, one and then another. The full moon rose. Under its silver light the Master and the twelve sat down on the hillside.
ch17.b041: Nathaniel gazed down at the city for a long time. It was beautiful. The word that this beauty would fall pressed on something in his chest. He loved philosophy, and he was used to thinking about things that pass away. But that had been passing away in books. These white stones in front of him, that golden roof — his people had looked on them for a thousand years. At last he asked how they would know when such things were about to come to pass.
ch17.b042: The Master answered. He was about to leave them, he said; he was going to the Father. After he was gone, many would come claiming to be deliverers and would lead many astray, and they must not be deceived. When they heard of wars and rumors of wars they were not to be alarmed. For the gospel’s sake they would be thrown out of the synagogues and put in prison, and some of them would be killed. But his spirit would not forsake them.
ch17.b043: Andrew asked: if the city and the temple were to be destroyed, and the Master was no longer there to direct them, when should they leave Jerusalem?
ch17.b044: As soon as he had asked it, Andrew was startled at himself. It was a chief’s question. He had already been reckoning the time after the Master was gone, the day he would have to lead his brothers without him. This was the first time he had said that reckoning out loud. The Master told them that when they saw Jerusalem surrounded by Roman armies they should flee to the mountains, and stay behind for nothing.
ch17.b045: The apostles sat silent in the moonlight for a long while. Years later, the believers remembered this warning, and when the Roman troops first appeared they left Jerusalem and found refuge in Pella.
ch17.b046: Late that night, on the way back to the camp, the thirteen walked without a word. And somewhere in that walking Judas finally confirmed his decision to abandon his brethren. He looked at the eleven backs in the moonlight — Peter, Andrew, the twins. They were walking along knowing nothing. Judas felt a little sorry for them. And the pity pleased him, because it seemed to set him on a higher place than theirs.
ch17.b047: At that hour the Sanhedrin was in session. Just before midnight they voted, unanimously, to put both Jesus and Lazarus to death. Their officers were to be ordered to take him not in public but in secret, by night if they could. The council agreed to meet again at ten the next morning at the home of Caiaphas the high priest, and adjourned.
ch17.b048: The Boy Who Would Not Let Go of the Basket
ch17.b049: Wednesday was a day of rest. Breakfast came later than usual, and an ominous silence lay over the camp. For a long time after the meal began no one spoke. At last the Master told them to rest that day, to think over everything that had happened since they came to Jerusalem and to ponder what lay ahead. He told Andrew that he himself would be away for the day; the apostles might spend the time as each of them chose, but on no account were they to go inside the gates of Jerusalem.
ch17.b050: David Zebedee offered to send three armed Galileans with him, but the Master declined. No one, he said, would lay hands on him until the hour when he was ready to lay down his life in keeping with his Father’s will. Then John Mark came out with a small basket of food and water. The Master smiled and reached for it, but the boy did not let go. When the Master went aside to pray, he said, he would stay quietly by the basket; he would ask no questions. For a while the two of them stood there, both holding on to the basket. At last the Master let go, and told the lad that since he longed with all his heart to come along, it would not be refused him. The two of them set off together into the hills.
ch17.b051: Watching, Nathaniel nearly laughed out loud. Then the laughter left him. The boy had not let go of the basket. And we just stood there.
ch17.b052: The apostles spent most of the day wandering over Olivet and visiting the disciples who were camped with them. By early afternoon they were longing for the Master to come back. As the hours went by they grew more and more anxious. There was a great deal of talk about whether he should have been allowed to go off alone into the hills with only an errand boy for company. No one said it aloud, but every one of them except Judas Iscariot wished he had been in John Mark’s place.
ch17.b053: In the middle of the afternoon Nathaniel spoke to about half a dozen apostles and as many disciples. The trouble with most of us, he said, is that we are halfhearted. We do not love the Master the way he loves us. If all of us had wanted to go with him the way John Mark did, he would surely have taken us all. When the boy held out the basket we just stood by; when the Master took hold of it, the boy would not let go. And so the Master went off into the hills with the basket and the boy and all, and we were left behind.
ch17.b054: When he had finished, Nathaniel looked around at the faces in the circle. No one was smiling. He started to add a joke and thought better of it. This was not a day a joke could ease. He noticed that not all twelve were there. Peter and John had been closeted for hours with the Greeks. And Judas was nowhere to be seen. Nathaniel could not remember having seen him since morning. He thought little of it. Judas was always off somewhere, reckoning something.
ch17.b055: Andrew could not think little of it. All through the afternoon, as the sun went down the sky, he looked for Judas again and again. He was not in the camp, not in the disciples’ tents, not on the slope toward the Kidron. Andrew looked down toward Jerusalem. *Do not go within the gates.* That morning the Master had told him directly, and he had passed the word to the others. Andrew did not want to believe that Judas had disobeyed. So he did not let himself believe it. He sat down on a rock and folded his hands on his knees. *Keep a firm hold on your brethren.* Yesterday morning’s words came back to him. But what of the brother your hand cannot reach?
ch17.b057: Judas Iscariot had vanished from the camp shortly after the Master and John Mark left that morning. He knew perfectly well that the Master had told them plainly not to go into Jerusalem. Even as he heard the words, he was already working out his route. A little after ten o’clock an informal meeting of the Sanhedrin convened at the home of Caiaphas the high priest. They were there to discuss what charges should be laid against Jesus, and how to bring him before the Roman authorities so that the death sentence they had already passed might be confirmed.
ch17.b058: As Judas walked toward the house of Caiaphas, his heart was churning on many levels at once. He had already decided to leave the movement. But that was not enough. He found himself suddenly and strangely resentful that the Master had never given him a place of greater honor. Treasurer. He had always been grateful for that office. Now it felt like proof that he had never been truly seen. And then there were Peter and James and John, the three who were always at the Master’s side. As he approached the high priest’s door, the hottest thing in Judas’s heart was not the thought of handing over the Master but the wish to get even with those three. And beneath that a new thought lifted its head. The honor he had failed to win in the new kingdom he could win in the old order — and win it now. If he could have both together, so much the better. It was not about money. Judas was not thinking of money.
ch17.b059: His cousin presented him to Caiaphas and the rulers. The cousin explained that Judas had come to see his mistake in letting himself be drawn in by the subtle teaching of Jesus, and that he now wished to break openly with the Galilean and be received back into the trust of his Judean brethren. Judas recognized, the cousin went on, that it would be best for the peace of Israel if Jesus were taken into custody; and as a token of his regret and of his sincerity, he had come to offer to work with the captain who held the orders for the arrest, so that Jesus might be seized quietly, without stirring up the crowds and without waiting until after the Passover.
ch17.b060: When his cousin had finished, Judas stepped forward before the high priest.
ch17.b061: “All that my cousin has promised, I will do. But what will you give me for it?”
ch17.b062: Across the cold, vain face of Caiaphas passed a look of contempt, something very near disgust. Judas did not see it. Or he saw it and did not recognize it. His heart was too deeply bent toward his own glory and his own advancement. All his life he had misread the words and faces of his friends. Today he misread the face of an enemy.
ch17.b063: Caiaphas looked down at him and told him to go to the captain of the guard and arrange with him to bring his Master to them that night or the next, and that when he had delivered him into their hands he would receive his reward. Judas withdrew and sat down with the captain of the temple guards. Jesus was not at the camp just then, and there was no knowing when he would return. So they agreed to take him the following evening, Thursday, after the people of the city and the pilgrims had all gone to sleep.
ch17.b064: Judas came back to the camp late in the afternoon, drunk on a sense of grandeur he had not felt for many days. He had come to Jesus dreaming of being a great man in the new kingdom. That kingdom was not coming. But he had been shrewd enough, he believed, to trade his disappointment for honor in the old order. He was certain that order would survive, and that it would destroy Jesus and everything he stood for.
ch17.b065: On the slope leading up to the camp he saw Andrew sitting on a rock. Andrew looked up. Judas smiled. He did not smile too late, nor too briefly. He smiled perfectly. Andrew nodded in answer to the smile. And it was the very perfection of it that troubled him. But once again he asked nothing.
ch17.b067: The Master did not come back with John Mark until after sunset. Since their return John Mark had been ominously silent. However hard anyone pressed him, all he would make plain was that the Master had told him not to speak. The Master talked with the Greeks. Had it not been that his apostles and disciples were already so unsettled, he would have ordained them, as he had once ordained the seventy.
ch17.b068: Wednesday evening was a time for being together. The Master did his best to lift the spirits of his downcast apostles, and it was all but impossible. Even when he went back over their years together, those full and loving days, they could not smile. He asked carefully after the families of each of them — Peter’s wife and children, Thomas’s household, the twins’ mother. Then he asked David Zebedee whether anyone had heard lately from his mother, or his youngest sister, or any of his family. David looked down at his feet. He was afraid to answer. A few days before, on his own initiative, he had sent word to his mother to bring the Master’s mother and his whole family to Jerusalem. He alone knew that they were on the way.
ch17.b069: It was then that the Master warned them not to rely on the support of the crowds. He reminded them of Galilee, where great throngs had followed them eagerly and then turned away just as eagerly. Those who knew the gospel only in their minds, and had never felt it in their hearts, could not be counted on when real trouble came. When the rulers struck with one accord against the Son of Man, he said, the multitude would either scatter in fear or stand by in silence. And he added that some who had been very close to them had already made up their minds to desert.
ch17.b070: The fireside went still. Only the crackle of the burning wood could be heard. The apostles did not look at one another. No one asked whom he meant. Nathaniel thought of the disciples who had left them at Pella, of half the crowd that had turned back at the Bethany ford. Probably those, he thought.
ch17.b071: Andrew could not think so. He looked across the fire at Judas. Judas was looking into the flames. His face was calm. The firelight lit one half of it, and the other half was in shadow. It had been just so, three years before, in Zebedee’s garden. Andrew remembered that night. He remembered too that he had not gone over to Judas, sitting alone under the fig tree. Now, again, he did not stand up. What would he say? Something he could not be sure of, something without proof? He sat with his hands folded on his knees. How he would think, all his life, about not rising that night, the Andrew of that night did not know.
ch17.b072: Even after he had spoken, the Master looked at Judas just as he looked at the others. He did not avoid him, and he did not let his eyes rest on him. When he spoke to Judas, his voice was no different. Judas found that hard to bear. And so he read it as proof that the Master knew nothing. He was always a man who read things that way.
ch17.b073: The Master told them that they had rested today in preparation for the times that were already upon them. They must watch and pray, and be strong for the days that would come tomorrow.
ch17.b074: An unspeakable tension hung over the camp. Silent messengers came and went, speaking only with David Zebedee. Before the evening was over, some of them learned that Lazarus had fled Bethany in haste. Even the Master’s good cheer, his unusual warmth, frightened them. Each of them felt a terrible isolation closing around him. They did not know what was coming. They only knew that none of them was ready to meet it. That evening was the lowest point their spirits would reach before the Master’s death.
ch17.b075: A little before midnight he sent them off to bed. Go and sleep, he told them; peace be on them until they rose in the morning — one more day to do the Father’s will and to know the joy of being his sons. He knew that this was the last night he would ever sleep through on earth with the family he had chosen.
ch17.b076: One by one the apostles went off to their tents. The twins tended the fire to the end. Matthew paused at the mouth of his tent and looked up at the sky. The moon, a day past full, hung above the olive trees of Gethsemane. Somewhere, hidden, John Mark was keeping watch over the Master’s tent.
ch17.b077: Judas Iscariot lay down with the money bag for a pillow. He could not fall asleep at once. Now and then, very briefly, something pricked his heart. Something like shame. Each time, he told himself: in the last moment the man will use his power and save himself. He called Lazarus out of the tomb. Whatever I do, he will not be hurt. The thought covered him like a shield. Beneath that shield, at last, he slept.
ch17.b078: Andrew stayed awake far into the night. He sat outside his tent and counted, one by one, the sleeping breaths of the eleven. They were all there. All twelve of them were there. Even after he had made sure of it, he could not bring himself to get up for a long time.
ch17.b080: The events follow Papers 173–177: the Monday gathering at Simon’s house, the descent to the temple and Judas’s question (173:0.1–0.3); the temple trade and money-changing, the cleansing of the temple while the apostles never lifted a hand, the question of authority and the parables, the saying about destroying this temple, the charge to Andrew, Philip, and Thomas to set up the camp, and the silent Monday night (173:1.1–5.6); the Tuesday farewells and the personal word to each of the twelve (174:0.1–0.3); the talk on forgiveness, the questions in the temple, Philip and the Greeks, and the lunch at Joseph’s home (174:1–5); the last temple discourse with eleven apostles (175:0.1–1.25); the Sanhedrin’s death vote and arrest orders that night (175:3.1–3.3, 175:4.13); Judas lunching with Sadducean relatives, missing the appeal to mercy and hearing only the denunciation (175:4.1); Matthew pointing to the temple buildings, the questions of Nathaniel and Andrew on Olivet by moonlight, the later flight to Pella, and Judas confirming his decision on the walk back (176:0.1–1.5, 176:2.9); the Wednesday rest, the order not to enter the city, David’s offer of guards, John Mark’s basket, the apostles’ wish to be in John Mark’s place, Nathaniel’s speech on “Supreme Desire,” and David’s summoning of the family (177:0.1–3.6); Judas’s bargain at the home of Caiaphas, his motives, the agreement on a Thursday-night arrest, and his return drunk with grandeur (177:4.1–4.12); and the Wednesday evening gathering, the inquiries after the families, the warning against trusting the crowds, the remark about those who had already decided to desert, the low ebb of that evening, and the midnight good night (177:5.1–5.6).
ch17.b081: Character details come from Paper 139 and related passages: Andrew’s early awareness of Judas’s trouble, which he kept to himself (139:1.8); Andrew confiding his serious doubts to no one on the day of the entry, unaware that Peter wore a sword (172:5.2); Judas’s habits of self-deception, of misreading his friends, and of nursing revenge (139:12.2, 139:12.6); his grudge against the three apostles, and the fact that money was not his motive (139:12.5, 177:4.4); the thought, used as a shield, that Jesus would save himself by his power at the last moment (139:12.12); Jesus loving and trusting Judas as he did the others (177:4.10); and Nathaniel’s humor and pride (139:6).
ch17.b082: Added fiction includes the apostles’ inner thoughts and feelings; the scenery of Olivet and the temple court; Nathaniel’s unspoken joke; Andrew counting the empty place at Joseph’s house and searching for Judas on Wednesday; Judas and Andrew meeting on the slope; Judas savoring his relative’s words; and Andrew counting the sleepers’ breathing on the last night. Judas’s words to Caiaphas are freshly rendered from the sense of the text; because the text does not name the sum at this point, no amount is given. The firelight on half of Judas’s face and the figure under the fig tree carry forward a scene planted in Chapter 4, “The Day of Ordination.”
ch17.b083: The words of Jesus are retold, not quoted, following the sense of the text.
